MUSA 5080 · Fall 2026

Author

Claudia Ashworth

Published

November 24, 2026

The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being rearrested within three years. The department has two proposed uses:

  • Use A: people above a threshold get more restrictive supervision (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
  • Use B: people above a threshold get priority for reentry services (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model will not use race. You’ve been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

What you’re turning in: this rendered document, published in the assignments/ folder of your portfolio.

How this assignment works: it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The Week 11 lab (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

A5 part Week 11 lab step
3.1 odds ratios Step 3
4.1 predictions + confusion matrix Steps 4–5
4.3 threshold sweep Step 5 (rates_at())
4.4 ROC + AUC Step 6
5.1–5.2 errors by race Step 7
5.3 what carries race in Step 8

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called recid (not two_year_recid), and you fit on train and evaluate on test. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every predict() in Parts 4 and 5 needs newdata = test.

The data

The National Institute of Justice’s Recidivism Forecasting Challenge data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Download the CSV from Canvas, put it in your portfolio’s data/ folder, and rename it nij_recidivism.csv.

A few things to know before you start:

  • Race is recorded only as Black or white. The data includes no one else.
  • Counts are top-coded: “10 or more” prior felony arrests is stored as text. parse_number() turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
  • Residence_PUMA is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia’s PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can’t map it.
  • Training_Sample is NIJ’s own train/test split. Use it.

Part 1: Load and clean

Code 
library(tidyverse)

nij <- read_csv("/Users/Claudia/Documents/GitHub/MUSA-5080-portfolio/docs/data/nij_recidivism.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years == "Yes"),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA)
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)

There are 3,167 missing values in the Gang Affiliated Column, all of which are female. If this variable were added to a regression model without addressing the missing values, R would automatically exclude those observations through complete-case analysis. This would disproportionately reduce the number of women in the sample, potentially introducing gender bias and affecting the accuracy of the model.

2.2 Pick one variable from the right-hand column and explain, in two sentences, why including it would make your model look better than it really is.

Including Violations_FailToReport would make the model appear more accurate because it provides information about a person’s behavior during parole supervision, which may be directly related to their likelihood of recidivism. However, this information would not have been available at the time of release, meaning the model is using future information to predict an outcome and artificially inflating its predictive accuracy.

The exponentiated coefficient for prior felony arrests is 1.18. This means that each additional felony arrest multiplies the odds of rearrest by about 18%, holding all other variables constant.

3.2 Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use predict(..., type = "response") with newdata to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

  • a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
  • a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person’s probability? Why are the two changes different?

Code 
people <- tibble(
  male               = c(1, 1),
  age_group          = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years       = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests  = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)

p_before <- predict(base_fit, newdata = people, type = "response")

people_plus_one <- people %>% mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests + 1)
p_after <- predict(base_fit, newdata = people_plus_one, type = "response")

tibble(
  person = c("Age 23-27", "Age 48+"),
  p_before = p_before,
  p_after = p_after,
  change = p_after - p_before
)
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  person    p_before p_after change
  <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Age 23-27    0.564   0.605 0.0406
2 Age 48+      0.179   0.204 0.0259

An additional arrest has the same effect on both individuals’ odds of rearrest, increasing them by a factor of 1.18. However, this does not translate into an equal change in their predicted probabilities. Because logistic regression follows a nonlinear, S-shaped relationship, changes in probability are more pronounced for individuals whose initial likelihood of rearrest is closer to 50%. This explains why the individual starting at an 18% probability experienced only a 2-percentage-point increase, while the individual starting at 56% saw a larger increase of approximately 5 percentage points.

3.3 Improve the model. Add at least three predictors from your “known at release” list. Keep race out. Call it my_fit. In two or three sentences, say what you added and why you expected each one to help.

WarningCheck for missing values before you add a variable

Some columns have blanks: Prison_Offense is missing for about 1 in 8 people, and Supervision_Level_First for about 1 in 15. If you add one as it is, glm() silently drops those people from training, and predict() returns NA for them in test. Then mean() gives NA in Parts 4–6, and table() quietly leaves them out. Either leave the variable out, or keep the blanks as their own category, for example mutate(offense = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing")). Whichever you choose, say so in your answer.

Code 
my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests + Condition_MH_SA + Education_Level,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(my_fit)

The variables I added are whether the individual struggles with mental health or substance abuse and education level. I chose prior mental health and substance abuse because they commonly connected to one another, and individuals who struggle with either are often over criminalized. I chose education level because it is deeply tied to class, which is a predictor for rates of incarceration. I did not drop any data.

Part 4: Choosing a threshold

4.1 Add a column p_hat to test with predicted probabilities from my_fit, and a column pred_50 that flags anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

Code 
test <- test %>%
  mutate(
    p_hat   = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
    pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5)
  )

table(test$pred_50 == "1")

FALSE  TRUE 
 2312  5495
Code 
table(test$Recidivism_Within_3years == "Yes")

FALSE  TRUE 
 3324  4483

4.2 What share of the test set does your model label “high risk” at 0.5? Compare it to the share actually rearrested. What does that tell you about 0.5 as a default for this data?

The test model labels 5,495 as high risk with a threshold of .5. This is compared to the 4,483 individuals who were actually rearrested within three years of release. This tells us that the model over predicts the number of people to be rearrested within three years.

4.3 Compute sensitivity and specificity for every threshold from 0.30 to 0.80 in steps of 0.05, and plot both lines on one chart with threshold on the x-axis.

Hint: in the lab you called rates_at() three times by hand. Here you need eleven thresholds. map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) ...) runs the same code once per threshold and stacks the results into one data frame. Your version will need p_hat instead of pred, and recid instead of two_year_recid.

Code 
thresholds <- seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.05)

sweep <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  pred <- as.integer(test$p_hat >= t)
  tibble(
    threshold   = t,
    sensitivity = sum(pred == 1 & test$recid == 1) / sum(test$recid == 1),
    specificity = sum(pred == 0 & test$recid == 0) / sum(test$recid == 0)
  )
})

4.4 Plot the ROC curve for my_fit on the test set with pROC and report the AUC. In one sentence: what does the AUC tell you, and what doesn’t it tell you about the decision the department has to make?

Code 
library(pROC)

roc_obj <- roc(response = test$recid, predictor = test$p_hat)

auc(roc_obj)
Area under the curve: 0.7032
Code 
ggroc(roc_obj, legacy.axes = TRUE) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 − specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)",
       title = "Sensitivity/Specificity Graph") +
  theme_minimal()

The AUC of 0.7032 suggests that the model has a moderate ability to distinguish between individuals who are re-incarcerated and those who do not, but it does not tell the department which probability threshold to use when making supervision decisions or how to balance the consequences of false positives and false negatives.

Part 5: Is it race-blind?

Race isn’t in your model. Now check the errors by race on the test set.

5.1 At the threshold of 0.5, compute for each race: the share labeled high risk, the share actually rearrested, the false positive rate (labeled high risk, not rearrested, out of everyone not rearrested), and the false negative rate.

Code 
test %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  summarize(
    n               = n(),
    share_high_risk = mean(pred_50 == 1),
    share_rearrested = mean(recid == 1),
    fpr = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
    fnr = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1)
  )
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  Race      n share_high_risk share_rearrested   fpr   fnr

1 BLACK  4534           0.725            0.582 0.580 0.170
2 WHITE  3273           0.674            0.564 0.492 0.185

5.2 Repeat 5.1 at two other thresholds from your sweep. Does the gap between groups close, stay, or flip?

Code 
errors_by_race <- function(t) {
  test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(p_hat >= t)) %>%
    group_by(Race) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold        = t,
      n                = n(),
      share_high_risk  = mean(pred == 1),
      share_rearrested = mean(recid == 1),
      fpr = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      fnr = sum(pred == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1)
    )
}

Although race is not explicitly included as a predictor in the model, the model produces different predicted risk levels for the two racial groups represented. At every threshold, Black individuals are assigned higher predicted risks of rearrest than their white counterparts.For both groups, the share of individuals classified as high risk increases as the threshold decreases. However, the difference between the two groups is smaller at a threshold of 0.7 than at 0.5, where the gap is approximately 4 percentage points. When the threshold decreases further to 0.03, the difference narrows slightly, to approximately 3 percentage points.

Part 6: Does it hold up in places it hasn’t seen?

Use leave-one-PUMA-group-out cross-validation on the training set, the same recipe as Week 10’s leave-one-district-out.

Code 
pumas <- levels(train$puma)

cv_puma <- map_dfr(pumas, function(u) {
  cv_train <- train %>% filter(puma != u)
  cv_test  <- train %>% filter(puma == u)

  fit <- glm(formula(my_fit), family = binomial, data = cv_train)

  cv_test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(predict(fit, newdata = cv_test,
                                     type = "response") >= 0.5)) %>%
    summarize(puma       = u,
              n          = n(),
              share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"),
              accuracy   = mean(pred == recid),
              fpr        = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0))
})

6.1 Plot each PUMA group’s false positive rate against its share of Black parolees. What pattern, if any, do you see?

Code 
ggplot(cv_puma, aes(x = share_black, y = fpr)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "False Positive Rate vs. Share of Black Parolees by PUMA",
       x = "Share of parolees who are Black",
       y = "False positive rate",
       size = "Parolees in PUMA")

There is a positive linear relationship between false positive rate and share of parolees who are Black.

6.2 If you put puma itself into the model as a predictor, would that make the model more or less race-blind? Make an argument using what you found in 6.1. (You may test it, but you don’t have to.)

If I were to put ‘puma’ into the model as a predictor, I would assume it would make the model less race-blind because are historically racially segregated.

Part 7: The memo

Write a memo (400–600 words) to the Department of Community Supervision. It must:

  1. Pick a threshold for Use A and a threshold for Use B, and defend each using the cost of a false positive and a false negative in that use. Cite your own numbers from Parts 4 and 5.
  2. Tell them whether “the model doesn’t use race” means it treats Black and white parolees the same, using your Part 5 results.
  3. End with one sentence: “I would / would not deploy this for Use , unless .”

The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being rearrested within three years. The department has two proposed uses:

  • Use A: people above a threshold get more restrictive supervision (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
  • Use B: people above a threshold get priority for reentry services (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model will not use race. You’ve been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

What you’re turning in: this rendered document, published in the assignments/ folder of your portfolio.

Write to a deputy commissioner, not to a statistician. No code, no jargon you haven’t explained.

Dear Deputy Commissioner,

The risk model developed for the Department of Community Supervision has some potential to inform parole decisions, but its effectiveness depends on how the department intends to use its predictions. Although the model demonstrates a moderate ability to distinguish between individuals who will and will not be rearrested within three years (AUC = 0.7032), it is important to recognize that its predictions are not equally useful for every decision. In particular, I would recommend using different thresholds depending on whether the model is being used to determine supervision requirements or to prioritize re-entry services.

For Use A, I would recommend a relatively high threshold of 0.7 before assigning individuals to more restrictive supervision. A false positive in this context could have serious consequences, as an individual who would not otherwise be rearrested could face increased surveillance, electronic monitoring, and a greater likelihood of revocation. These consequences could unnecessarily limit an individual’s freedom and make successful reintegration more difficult. While a higher threshold will inevitably produce more false negatives, the consequences of incorrectly imposing restrictive supervision make it important to prioritize reducing false positives. The department should be particularly cautious about treating a predicted probability as sufficient justification for imposing additional restrictions.

For Use B, I would recommend a lower threshold of 0.3 to identify individuals who should receive priority for reentry services. Unlike restrictive supervision, providing additional resources to someone who is not ultimately rearrested does not carry the same negative consequences. In fact, access to housing assistance, employment opportunities, and case management could benefit individuals regardless of their predicted likelihood of rearrest. A lower threshold would also reduce the number of individuals who are overlooked and could benefit from these services. Although this approach would produce more false positives, the potential benefit of connecting more individuals with resources outweighs the relatively low cost of providing assistance to someone who may not be rearrested.

It is also important to recognize that excluding race from the model does not mean that Black and white parolees are treated equally by its predictions. Although race was not explicitly included as a predictor, the model still produced different predicted risk levels across the two racial groups represented in the data. At each threshold, Black individuals were more likely to be classified as high risk than their white counterparts. My findings also showed that the difference between the share of individuals classified as high risk varied across thresholds, with a gap of approximately four percentage points at 0.5. This suggests that other variables included in the model may indirectly carry information about race. For example, the distributions of prior misdemeanor arrests and prison offenses differed across racial groups. Additionally, my analysis found a positive relationship between the share of Black parolees in a geographic area and its false positive rate. These findings suggest that the model may reproduce existing racial disparities even without explicitly considering race.

Ultimately, the department should not interpret the exclusion of race as evidence that the model is free from racial bias. The model’s predictions should be evaluated alongside the consequences they produce for different populations, particularly when they influence decisions that restrict individual freedom.

I would not deploy this for Use A, unless the department first establishes stronger safeguards against racial disparities and ensures that model predictions are not used as the sole basis for restrictive supervision.

# The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being **rearrested within three years**. The department has two proposed uses:

- **Use A:** people above a threshold get **more restrictive supervision** (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
- **Use B:** people above a threshold get **priority for reentry services** (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model **will not use race**. You've been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

**What you're turning in:** this rendered document, published in the `assignments/` folder of your portfolio.

**How this assignment works:** it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The **Week 11 lab** (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

| A5 part | Week 11 lab step |
|---|---|
| 3.1 odds ratios | Step 3 |
| 4.1 predictions + confusion matrix | Steps 4–5 |
| 4.3 threshold sweep | Step 5 (`rates_at()`) |
| 4.4 ROC + AUC | Step 6 |
| 5.1–5.2 errors by race | Step 7 |
| 5.3 what carries race in | Step 8 |

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called **`recid`** (not `two_year_recid`), and you **fit on `train` and evaluate on `test`**. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every `predict()` in Parts 4 and 5 needs `newdata = test`.


# The data

The National Institute of Justice's **Recidivism Forecasting Challenge** data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Download the CSV from Canvas, put it in your portfolio's `data/` folder, and rename it `nij_recidivism.csv`.

A few things to know before you start:

- **Race is recorded only as Black or white.** The data includes no one else.
- **Counts are top-coded:** "10 or more" prior felony arrests is stored as text. `parse_number()` turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
- **`Residence_PUMA`** is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia's PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can't map it.
- **`Training_Sample`** is NIJ's own train/test split. Use it.

# Part 1: Load and clean


```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)

nij <- read_csv("/Users/Claudia/Documents/GitHub/MUSA-5080-portfolio/docs/data/nij_recidivism.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years == "Yes"),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA)
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)
```

**1.1** How many people are in `train` and in `test`? What share of each was rearrested within three years?

table(train$Recidivism_Within_3years)

nrow(test)
table(test$Recidivism_Within_3years)

```
*There are 7,807 people in test, 4,483 of which were rearrested within three years. The population is 57.2% of the population in the entire test. In train, there are 18,028 total people in wich 57.8% (10,421) of them were rearrested within three years.*  

**1.2** Look at `Gang_Affiliated`. How many values are missing, and who are they? (Hint: cross-tabulate it with `Gender`.) What would happen to your sample if you added this variable to a model without handling the missing values?

library(dplyr)

str(train$Gang_Affiliated)
str(train$Gender)
table(train$Gang_Affiliated, train$Gender, useNA = "ifany")
```

*There are 3,167 missing values in the Gang Affiliated Column, all of which are female. If this variable were added to a regression model without addressing the missing values, R would automatically exclude those observations through complete-case analysis. This would disproportionately reduce the number of women in the sample, potentially introducing gender bias and affecting the accuracy of the model.*

# Part 3: Build a race-blind model

Start from this model.

```{r}
#| label: base-model
base_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(base_fit)
```

**3.1** Exponentiate the coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for `prior_fel_arrests` in one sentence, using the word *odds* correctly.

```{r}
exp(coef(base_fit))
```

*The exponentiated coefficient for prior felony arrests is 1.18. This means that each additional felony arrest multiplies the odds of rearrest by about 18%, holding all other variables constant.* 

**3.2** Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use `predict(..., type = "response")` with `newdata` to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

- a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
- a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person's probability? Why are the two changes different?

```{r}
people <- tibble(
  male               = c(1, 1),
  age_group          = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years       = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests  = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)

p_before <- predict(base_fit, newdata = people, type = "response")

people_plus_one <- people %>% mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests + 1)
p_after <- predict(base_fit, newdata = people_plus_one, type = "response")

tibble(
  person = c("Age 23-27", "Age 48+"),
  p_before = p_before,
  p_after = p_after,
  change = p_after - p_before
)
```

*An additional arrest has the same effect on both individuals' odds of rearrest, increasing them by a factor of 1.18. However, this does not translate into an equal change in their predicted probabilities. Because logistic regression follows a nonlinear, S-shaped relationship, changes in probability are more pronounced for individuals whose initial likelihood of rearrest is closer to 50%. This explains why the individual starting at an 18% probability experienced only a 2-percentage-point increase, while the individual starting at 56% saw a larger increase of approximately 5 percentage points.* 

**3.3** Improve the model. Add at least **three** predictors from your "known at release" list. Keep race out. Call it `my_fit`. In two or three sentences, say what you added and why you expected each one to help.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check for missing values before you add a variable
Some columns have blanks: `Prison_Offense` is missing for about 1 in 8 people, and `Supervision_Level_First` for about 1 in 15. If you add one as it is, `glm()` **silently drops** those people from training, and `predict()` returns `NA` for them in `test`. Then `mean()` gives `NA` in Parts 4–6, and `table()` quietly leaves them out. Either leave the variable out, or keep the blanks as their own category, for example `mutate(offense = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing"))`. Whichever you choose, say so in your answer.
:::

```{r}
#| label: my-model
my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests + Condition_MH_SA + Education_Level,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(my_fit)
```

*The variables I added are whether the individual struggles with mental health or substance abuse and education level. I chose prior mental health and substance abuse because they commonly connected to one another, and individuals who struggle with either are often over criminalized. I chose education level because it is deeply tied to class, which is a predictor for rates of incarceration. I did not drop any data.*    

# Part 4: Choosing a threshold

**4.1** Add a column `p_hat` to `test` with predicted probabilities from `my_fit`, and a column `pred_50` that flags anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

```{r}
test <- test %>%
  mutate(
    p_hat   = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
    pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5)
  )

table(test$pred_50 == "1")

table(test$Recidivism_Within_3years == "Yes")
```


**4.2** What share of the test set does your model label "high risk" at 0.5? Compare it to the share actually rearrested. What does that tell you about 0.5 as a default for this data?

*The test model labels 5,495 as high risk with a threshold of .5. This is compared to the 4,483 individuals who were actually rearrested within three years of release. This tells us that the model over predicts the number of people to be rearrested within three years.* 

**4.3** Compute sensitivity and specificity for every threshold from 0.30 to 0.80 in steps of 0.05, and plot both lines on one chart with threshold on the x-axis.

Hint: in the lab you called `rates_at()` three times by hand. Here you need eleven thresholds. `map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) ...)` runs the same code once per threshold and stacks the results into one data frame. Your version will need `p_hat` instead of `pred`, and `recid` instead of `two_year_recid`.

```{r}
thresholds <- seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.05)

sweep <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  pred <- as.integer(test$p_hat >= t)
  tibble(
    threshold   = t,
    sensitivity = sum(pred == 1 & test$recid == 1) / sum(test$recid == 1),
    specificity = sum(pred == 0 & test$recid == 0) / sum(test$recid == 0)
  )
})

sweep

sweep %>%
  pivot_longer(c(sensitivity, specificity),
               names_to = "measure", values_to = "rate") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = threshold, y = rate, color = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = thresholds) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = "Rate", color = NULL,
       title = "Sensitivity and specificity across thresholds") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.4** Plot the ROC curve for `my_fit` on the test set with `pROC` and report the AUC. In one sentence: what does the AUC tell you, and what doesn't it tell you about the decision the department has to make?

```{r}
library(pROC)

roc_obj <- roc(response = test$recid, predictor = test$p_hat)

auc(roc_obj)

ggroc(roc_obj, legacy.axes = TRUE) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 − specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)",
       title = "Sensitivity/Specificity Graph") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*The AUC of 0.7032 suggests that the model has a moderate ability to distinguish between individuals who are re-incarcerated and those who do not, but it does not tell the department which probability threshold to use when making supervision decisions or how to balance the consequences of false positives and false negatives.* 

# Part 5: Is it race-blind?

Race isn't in your model. Now check the errors by race on the **test set**.

**5.1** At the threshold of 0.5, compute for each race: the share labeled high risk, the share actually rearrested, the **false positive rate** (labeled high risk, not rearrested, out of everyone not rearrested), and the **false negative rate**.

```{r}
test %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  summarize(
    n               = n(),
    share_high_risk = mean(pred_50 == 1),
    share_rearrested = mean(recid == 1),
    fpr = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
    fnr = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1)
  )
```

**5.2** Repeat 5.1 at two other thresholds from your sweep. Does the gap between groups close, stay, or flip?

```{r}
errors_by_race <- function(t) {
  test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(p_hat >= t)) %>%
    group_by(Race) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold        = t,
      n                = n(),
      share_high_risk  = mean(pred == 1),
      share_rearrested = mean(recid == 1),
      fpr = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      fnr = sum(pred == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1)
    )
}

errors_by_race(0.3)
```
```{r}
errors_by_race <- function(t) {
  test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(p_hat >= t)) %>%
    group_by(Race) %>%
    summarize(
      threshold        = t,
      n                = n(),
      share_high_risk  = mean(pred == 1),
      share_rearrested = mean(recid == 1),
      fpr = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
      fnr = sum(pred == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1)
    )
}

errors_by_race(0.7)
```
```{r}
view(errors_by_race(0.7))
view(errors_by_race(0.5))
view(errors_by_race(.3))
```

```{r}
combined <- bind_rows(errors_by_race(0.7), errors_by_race(0.5), errors_by_race(0.3), .id = "source")  
```

*Although race is not explicitly included as a predictor in the model, the model produces different predicted risk levels for the two racial groups represented. At every threshold, Black individuals are assigned higher predicted risks of rearrest than their white counterparts.For both groups, the share of individuals classified as high risk increases as the threshold decreases. However, the difference between the two groups is smaller at a threshold of 0.7 than at 0.5, where the gap is approximately 4 percentage points. When the threshold decreases further to 0.03, the difference narrows slightly, to approximately 3 percentage points.* 

**5.3** Investigate at least two candidates by comparing their distributions by race. Possibilities include age, prior arrests, prison offense, and place (`puma`). Show your evidence with a table or chart for each.

# Part 6: Does it hold up in places it hasn't seen?

Use leave-one-PUMA-group-out cross-validation **on the training set**, the same recipe as Week 10's leave-one-district-out.

```{r}
pumas <- levels(train$puma)

cv_puma <- map_dfr(pumas, function(u) {
  cv_train <- train %>% filter(puma != u)
  cv_test  <- train %>% filter(puma == u)

  fit <- glm(formula(my_fit), family = binomial, data = cv_train)

  cv_test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(predict(fit, newdata = cv_test,
                                     type = "response") >= 0.5)) %>%
    summarize(puma       = u,
              n          = n(),
              share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"),
              accuracy   = mean(pred == recid),
              fpr        = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0))
})
```

**6.1** Plot each PUMA group's false positive rate against its share of Black parolees. What pattern, if any, do you see?

```{r}
ggplot(cv_puma, aes(x = share_black, y = fpr)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "False Positive Rate vs. Share of Black Parolees by PUMA",
       x = "Share of parolees who are Black",
       y = "False positive rate",
       size = "Parolees in PUMA")
```

*There is a positive linear relationship between false positive rate and share of parolees who are Black.*  

**6.2** If you put `puma` itself into the model as a predictor, would that make the model more or less race-blind? Make an argument using what you found in 6.1. (You may test it, but you don't have to.)

*If I were to put 'puma' into the model as a predictor, I would assume it would make the model less race-blind because are historically racially segregated.*

Write a memo (**400–600 words**) to the Department of Community Supervision. It must:

1. **Pick a threshold for Use A and a threshold for Use B**, and defend each using the cost of a false positive and a false negative *in that use*. Cite your own numbers from Parts 4 and 5.
2. Tell them **whether "the model doesn't use race" means it treats Black and white parolees the same**, using your Part 5 results.

# The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being **rearrested within three years**. The department has two proposed uses:

- **Use A:** people above a threshold get **more restrictive supervision** (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
- **Use B:** people above a threshold get **priority for reentry services** (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model **will not use race**. You've been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

**What you're turning in:** this rendered document, published in the `assignments/` folder of your portfolio.


Write to a deputy commissioner, not to a statistician. No code, no jargon you haven't explained.

Dear Deputy Commissioner,

The risk model developed for the Department of Community Supervision has some potential to inform parole decisions, but its effectiveness depends on how the department intends to use its predictions. Although the model demonstrates a moderate ability to distinguish between individuals who will and will not be rearrested within three years (AUC = 0.7032), it is important to recognize that its predictions are not equally useful for every decision. In particular, I would recommend using different thresholds depending on whether the model is being used to determine supervision requirements or to prioritize re-entry services.

For Use A, I would recommend a relatively high threshold of 0.7 before assigning individuals to more restrictive supervision. A false positive in this context could have serious consequences, as an individual who would not otherwise be rearrested could face increased surveillance, electronic monitoring, and a greater likelihood of revocation. These consequences could unnecessarily limit an individual's freedom and make successful reintegration more difficult. While a higher threshold will inevitably produce more false negatives, the consequences of incorrectly imposing restrictive supervision make it important to prioritize reducing false positives. The department should be particularly cautious about treating a predicted probability as sufficient justification for imposing additional restrictions.

For Use B, I would recommend a lower threshold of 0.3 to identify individuals who should receive priority for reentry services. Unlike restrictive supervision, providing additional resources to someone who is not ultimately rearrested does not carry the same negative consequences. In fact, access to housing assistance, employment opportunities, and case management could benefit individuals regardless of their predicted likelihood of rearrest. A lower threshold would also reduce the number of individuals who are overlooked and could benefit from these services. Although this approach would produce more false positives, the potential benefit of connecting more individuals with resources outweighs the relatively low cost of providing assistance to someone who may not be rearrested.

It is also important to recognize that excluding race from the model does not mean that Black and white parolees are treated equally by its predictions. Although race was not explicitly included as a predictor, the model still produced different predicted risk levels across the two racial groups represented in the data. At each threshold, Black individuals were more likely to be classified as high risk than their white counterparts. My findings also showed that the difference between the share of individuals classified as high risk varied across thresholds, with a gap of approximately four percentage points at 0.5. This suggests that other variables included in the model may indirectly carry information about race. For example, the distributions of prior misdemeanor arrests and prison offenses differed across racial groups. Additionally, my analysis found a positive relationship between the share of Black parolees in a geographic area and its false positive rate. These findings suggest that the model may reproduce existing racial disparities even without explicitly considering race.

Ultimately, the department should not interpret the exclusion of race as evidence that the model is free from racial bias. The model's predictions should be evaluated alongside the consequences they produce for different populations, particularly when they influence decisions that restrict individual freedom.

I would not deploy this for Use A, unless the department first establishes stronger safeguards against racial disparities and ensures that model predictions are not used as the sole basis for restrictive supervision.
